a) we report the first case of unapparent hypoxantine guanine phosphoribosiltransferase (HPGT) deficiency; b) we report a new mutation in the HPGT gene, c.424 A> G (T142A); and c) we report that HPGT activity in intact erythroctes is a useful tool for the diagnosis of HPGT deficiency.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypoxanthine phosphoribose pyrophosphorylase activity is not a good marker for HPRT deficiency.
the determination of HPRT activity in intact erythroocytes may be a more sensitive test than in hemolysed cells for the diagnosis of partial HPRT deficiency.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, in case of clinical suspicion, HPRT activity should be assayed in erythrocytes, even if hemolysate activity is normal.
